paper_title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Medical large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) now achieve strong results in medical examinations, visual question answering, and broad benchmark suites [16]. However, exam-style accuracy offers limited insight into subspecialty care, where clinicians must synthesize disease-specific guidelines, multimodal evidence, and evolving patient states over time. During clinical apprenticeship, physicians do not learn these skills in isolation. Recalling clinical guideline is only the first step; specialists must also ground staging in diagnostic images, tailor treatment plans to patient constraints, and revise decisions as new responses or toxicities emerge. Evaluating medical AI therefore requires following this same progression from foundational knowledge to longitudinal Equal contribution. While isolated tasks can pinpoint weaknesses in individual skills, only linked patient episodes can reveal whether these skills succeed together for the same patient [79]. Evaluating the progression from individual competencies to integrated clinical care requires disease setting in which multimodal evidence and sequential decisions are closely connected. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), prevalent in Southern China and Southeast Asia [1012], is managed according to staging systems and clinical guidelines [1315]. Diagnosis, staging, and risk assessment require integrating histopathology, multi-sequence MRI, and plasma EBV DNA [11, 16]. Clinical evidence and management objectives vary across stages of care, with subsequent decisions shaped by both the current patient state and preceding clinical events. During treatment and follow-up, tumor response, treatment-related toxicities, and recurrence or progression may influence management strategies [12, 14, 15]. NPC therefore provides suitable setting for evaluating both individual specialist competencies and their integration across successive stages of care. To systematically assess these capabilities, we introduce NPCBench, clinical apprenticeship benchmark for NPC modeled on the progressive training of specialist physicians. As shown in Fig. 1, it organizes the evaluation into six progressive levels and an open-ended consultation suite. L1 and L2 test guideline recall and application. L3 tests pathology and MRI evidence grounding. L4 tests case planning from single patient state, L5 longitudinal decision revision, and L6 linked CarePath episodes. O1 evaluates rubric-based specialist consultation. By pairing component tasks with patient trajectories, NPCBench asks central measurement question: Are diagnostic and care answers jointly correct for the same patient when component scores are high? Models with similar average accuracy can exhibit different patient-level error patterns, or even select the right treatment 2 while misinterpreting the underlying MRI evidence. NPCBench therefore pairs task-level scores with strict patient-level correctness, while holding patients and questions fixed in matched controls to examine how visual evidence, clinical chronology, and answer formats shape model decisions. Using NPCBench, we investigate four research questions (RQ1RQ4) across 30 medical and generalpurpose models. RQ1 examines how well models translate guideline knowledge into case-level planning: guideline recall exceeds 92%, whereas the highest case-planning accuracy is 71.9%. RQ2 probes whether staging predictions are grounded in accurate visual interpretation: complete invasion correctness reaches at most 5.0% on the 100-patient anatomical panel, showing that correct stage labels often lack complete anatomical support. RQ3 examines decision revision and patient-level success: history can correct answers and introduce new errors. In CarePath, Gemini-3.1 achieves 89.9% Care accuracy but 11.0% Strict success; Claude-4.6 has the highest Strict success at 23.0%. RQ4 assesses consultation safety and automated judge reliability: GPT-5.1, the highest-scoring consultation model, triggers major-error criteria in 14.6% of responses under the primary judge, while rubric judges show sensitivityspecificity imbalances against physician annotations. We summarize the main contributions of this work as follows. ① clinical apprenticeship evaluation framework. We shift the evaluation focus from static answer correctness to pathway correctness. NPCBench assesses whether models make consistent clinical decisions across patient-state transitions, integrating guideline constraints, multimodal evidence grounding, and longitudinal disease evolution. ② specialist-curated multimodal and longitudinal dataset. We release 4,777 component and consultation items alongside 100 CarePath episodes with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks, unifying guideline rules, pathology slides, multi-sequence MRI scans, longitudinal EHR trajectories, and consultation rubrics within single oncology pathway. ③ Diagnostic dissection of the clinical composition gap. Across 30 models, we combine capability profiling with controlled interventions and physician-calibrated judging to identify where visual grounding separates from treatment decisions, how patient history changes decisions, and where high local scores coexist with patient-level errors.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: From exam QA to clinically structured benchmarks. Early evaluations of medical LLMs relied on static, examination-style questionanswering benchmarks, including MedQA [17], MedMCQA [18], PubMedQA [19], the medical subsets of MMLU [20], MultiMedQA [2], MedBench [21], CMB [22], and CMExam [23]. These benchmarks capture medical knowledge and local reasoning, but they do not test whether model can accumulate patient evidence, review decisions, and preserve coherence across the care pathway. Recent broad suites such as MedHELM [8], MedXpertQA [24], and AnesSuites AnesBench [25] move the evaluation toward clinically meaningful capabilities and Figure 2: Task composition of NPCBench. Evaluation items are distributed across six progressive levels (L1L6) and the open-ended consultation suite (O1). Hatched slices each account for less than 5% of their subset; L6 shows its 217 care decisions. More clinical category names are defined in Appendix A. 3 specialty-aware reasoning. NPCBench follows this direction and makes the clinical apprenticeship ladder explicit: it measures component skills alongside longitudinal decisions and episode-level care correctness. Multimodal, longitudinal, and rubric-based clinical evaluation. Medical MLLM benchmarks have expanded from image QA datasets such as VQA-RAD [26], SLAKE [27], and PathVQA [28] to broader evaluations of multimodality, trustworthiness, endoscopy, clinical reasoning, and sequence grounding [2933]. In parallel, HealthBench [34], LiveMedBench [35], LLMEval-Med [36], MedDialogRubrics [37], and ClinConsensus [38] use expert-validated rubrics or temporally grounded cases to evaluate open-ended clinical responses. Workflow-oriented resources such as MedJourney [39], MedAgentBench [40], MedAgentBoard [41], and MTBBench [42] further shift evaluation from static snapshots toward state transitions. NPCBench brings these directions into single disease setting: pathology and MRI evidence grounding, patient-level longitudinal revision, strict CarePath episodes, and criterion-level consultation rubrics. Appendix gives fuller comparison with recent medical benchmark families.

sections.title: 3.1 Overview
sections.content: NPCBench organizes the clinical apprenticeship framework into progressive capability ladder (L1L6) and cross-level consultation rubrics (O1). The ladder spans guideline memory, atomic application, multimodal evidence grounding, case-level planning, longitudinal decision revision, and linked care episodes. Lower levels (L1L4) assess individual capability components; L5L6 examine longitudinal decisions and joint diagnosticcare correctness within patients. O1 complements these tasks by assessing free-text consultation quality. These tasks assess whether specialist decisions follow guidelines, use multimodal evidence, and remain consistent with patients clinical course. Four design principles guide task construction and clinical review: (i) Competence isolation requires each level in the progressive capability ladder (L1L6) to measure distinct, clinically meaningful component of specialist competence. (ii) Evidence-boundary control fixes the available evidence at the intended clinical decision point, removing future treatment, outcomes, and other answer-leaking cues. (iii) Clinical determinacy requires reference decisions supported by guidelines or expert consensus, given the provided clinical evidence. (iv)Auditable open-ended scoring uses case-specific consultation rubrics (O1) to assess clinical justification, evidence grounding, conditional reasoning, and safety. All patient materials are de-identified, and NPC oncologists verified component validity, decision determinacy, and the fidelity of patient-state transitions. Figure 2 shows the composition of each subset, and Fig. 3 illustrates the pipeline for constructing L1L5 items.

sections.title: 3.2 Construction and Validation
sections.content: Expert-curated clinical materials are converted into standardized evaluation items and reference answers. L1L2 were derived from CSCO and NCCN guidelines; L3 from pathology and multisequence MRI images; and L4L6 and O1 from de-identified real-world patient records, covering caselevel planning, longitudinal decision-making, full CarePath evaluation, and open-ended consultations with scoring rubrics. Multidisciplinary reviewers in oncology, pathology, and radiology assessed clinical validity, evidence sufficiency, and reference standards. For L1L2, experts verified guideline consistency and answer determinacy; for L3, they validated pathology labels, MRI sequence and anatomical structure identification, invasion status, and T/N staging against imaging evidence. For L4, they assessed case sufficiency and appropriateness of reference decisions given patient-specific clinical states; for L5L6, they verified evidence from decision-points, reference actions, and transitions from clinical state; and for O1, they reviewed core clinical requirements, supporting evidence, conditional recommendations, and major/minor error criteria to ensure clinically valid and auditable scoring.

sections.title: 3.3 Evaluation Levels and Scoring Units
sections.content: L1.G-Mem: Guideline memory. The 250 expert-reviewed questions assess NPC guideline knowledge: 153 have both CSCO and NCCN support, 80 CSCO support only, and 17 NCCN support only. 4 Figure 3: Construction of the L1L5 component tasks. Guideline questions, image tasks, and clinical checkpoints undergo specialist review of the available evidence and reference answers. They probe treatment indications, staging implications, recommendation boundaries, surveillance, and contraindications. Item accuracy is the primary endpoint. L2.A-App: Atomic guideline application. The 185 short-vignette questions cover initial definitive management, recurrence, metastatic/systemic management, and toxicity or contraindications. The main score averages accuracy over these four capability groups, giving each group equal weight. L3.MM-EG: Multimodal evidence grounding. Pathology contains 69 overview cases (39 NPCpositive and 30 negative). MRI comprises 200 sequence-recognition questions, 400 T-stage cases, and 400 N-stage cases, with patient-disjoint and cohorts. Within the 400 T-stage cases, 100-patient anatomical panel provides 2,700 structure cards covering 18 base structures, evaluating both structure identification and tumor invasion assessment. Overall, we report pathology, MRI sequence, structure-identification, T-stage, and N-stage accuracy separately, with additional metrics for invasion accuracy, joint structureinvasion correctness, and evidence-grounded T-stage success. L4.C-Plan: Case-level planning. The 165 questions cover 84 patient groups and provide clinical snapshots of stage, treatment history, response, organ function, and other relevant constraints. Plausible alternative plans test whether model identifies the next action appropriate to that specific state. Patient-macro accuracy weights patients equally. L5.L-Rev: Longitudinal revision. The 305 questions cover 100 trajectories with one to five scored checkpoints at treatment, reassessment, toxicity, recurrence, or follow-up. Each checkpoint requires interpreting new findings in the context of earlier treatment and response. We report turn-micro accuracy and all-turn patient success. The primary task supplies full history in one prompt; matchedhistory and serial-interaction controls are evaluated separately. L6.CP-Epi: CarePath episodes. The 100-patient CarePath cohort comprises 417 tasks: 100 pathology assessments, 100 MRI T-stage assessments, and 217 care decisions. Clinical records remain patient-linked; care-decision selection uses model-informed difficulty enrichment to prioritize clinical decisions that challenge models (Appendix C.3.5). Strict requires correct pathology, MRI T-stage, and every care answer; structure predictions provide auxiliary diagnostics. Each care question is answered independently with clinical context, incorporating the models pathology/T predictions and reference N/M/overall stages where required. O1.C-Rub: ConsultRubrics. The 103 consultation items span 42 patients and 1,726 rubric criteria: 1,069 positive requirements and 657 negative criteria. Satisfied positive requirements add weighted 5 credit; triggered major and minor errors deduct two and one points, respectively. The sum is floored at zero after item-level aggregation, normalized to 0100, and averaged over all 103 item scores. The primary judge and physician calibration are described below.

sections.title: 4.2 Guideline Knowledge and Case Planning
sections.content: Table 1 summarizes model performance across all benchmark tasks. Addressing RQ1, we examine how foundational guideline competence translates into case-level planning. Although Gemini3.1-Pro-Preview leads the guideline recall with 94.0% and the atomic application with 92.5%, its precision drops to 71.9% in L4, followed by Claude-Sonnet-4.6 and Gemini-2.5-Pro. In addition, models with nearly identical L1 and L2 scoressuch as GPT-5.1 and DeepSeek-V3.1diverge sharply on L4 planning (63.5 vs. 51.8%). Although these subsets differ in item composition and weighting, this divergence shows that multi-factor case planning must be evaluated directly rather than inferred from guideline accuracy. Furthermore, paired comparison on 71 physician-audited L1 items reveals that even high guideline scores partly rely on multiple-choice cues: removing answer options while holding the target knowledge fixed lowers accuracy by 7.0 percentage points (pp) for Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview, 12.7 pp for GPT-4.1, and 15.5 pp for GPT-5.1 shown as in Figure. 7i.

In the CarePath cohort, Gemini-3.1 achieves the highest Care accuracy (195/217 decisions, 89.9%) and All-care success (83.0%), yet its Strict success is only 11.0%. In contrast, Claude-4.6 achieves lower Care (80.6%) and All-care (64.0%) but the highest Strict success (23.0%; exact 95% CI: 15.232.5%; Fig. 4ce). Thus care accuracy alone does not identify which models most often answer all diagnostic and care questions correctly for patient. Joint correctness identifies the patients behind this gap. For Gemini-3.1, 72 of 100 patients have all care decisions correct despite at least one incorrect pathology or MRI T-stage label; the corresponding number is 41 for Claude-4.6. Conversely, Hulu-Med32B has 38 patients with both diagnostic labels correct but at least one incorrect care decision (Fig. 6; Table A20). Care answers and diagnostic labels can therefore disagree in correctness. To further examine whether diagnostic evidence affects care decisions, we compare predicted and reference pathology, MRI T-stage, and invasion findings in 25 CarePath patients. Fourteen local models answer the same 146 care questions under both conditions, with other clinical context fixed. Patientaveraged care accuracy, excluding diagnostic scores, changes by 3.2 to +4.1 pp, with 12 of 14 intervals including zero (Fig. 7d; Table A23). Claude-4.6 scores 76.5% versus 84.3% for Care, but 68.0% versus 52.0% for All-care (Table A21). The groups contribute 102 and 115 decisions, respectively. Class imbalance also matters: constant T3 predictions score 58% in CarePath, above the best models 52%. The highest balanced accuracy is 30.5%, versus 25% for constant predictions (Table A19; Fig. A4). L3 therefore complements CarePaths joint endpoint with stage-discrimination and grounding tests. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: NPCBench links foundational guideline knowledge and multimodal image interpretation to longitudinal decision-making, joint patient-level correctness, and specialist consultation in NPC care. Evaluating 30 models reveals that local accuracy rarely guarantees coherent patient management: stage predictions frequently lack complete anatomical support, longitudinal history corrects prior mistakes while introducing new errors, and high-scoring consultations still trigger critical safety violations. On CarePath episodes, accurate treatment choices routinely coexist with flawed image interpretations, capping strict patient-level success at just 23.0% despite substantially higher decisionlevel accuracy. These findings establish evidencedecision consistency as central benchmark target: meaningful clinical progress requires models to ground interpretations in valid evidence and sustain accurate decisions across the entire course of care for the same patient. Limitations. Our evaluation is constrained by primarily single-center records, assigned pathology in 75 model-selected CarePath episodes, score sensitivity to class balance and episode length, and the six-case Expanded Audit. Future more multi-center cohorts with fully patient-matched modalities and prospective studies are therefore needed to establish whether benchmark gains improve clinical care.

sections.content: The following sections describe the clinical sources, question construction, patient coverage, and reference annotations. Clinical data and ethics. The retrospective use of clinical data was approved under IRB protocol B2026-465-01. Patient materials follow the hospitals de-identification procedure. Direct identifiers and unnecessary location details are removed, and dates are expressed relative to the patients clinical course where appropriate. L4 retains clinical decision dates needed to identify the applicable guideline edition. Age and sex are retained when needed for reasoning. NPC oncology specialists review clinical validity, reference answers, supporting evidence, and transitions between care decisions. Task construction. L1 and L2 translate guideline knowledge and decision thresholds into questions with adjudicated answers. L4 combines diagnosis, stage, treatment history, response, toxicity, and patient-specific constraints into fixed-state planning cases. L5 organizes longitudinal records around clinical decision checkpoints, retaining the cumulative evidence available at each point and removing subsequent orders or outcomes that reveal the target decision. L6 links pathology, MRI, and selected care decisions within patient episodes. O1 uses consultation scenarios with separate criteria for core conclusions, supporting evidence, conditional reasoning, and clinically important errors. L1 retains item-level guideline references and supporting evidence. All 350 L2/L4 items include their construction sources and reviewed answer rationales. Source records distinguish the guideline edition stated in question from references supporting its answer: the former is available to the model, whereas the latter explains the reference decision. Recorded edition constraints occur in two L2 and four L4 questions and are included in the model inputs; edition and section references are available for subset of items. 16 Clinical review and answer format. The evaluated sets contain 250 L1, 185 L2, and 165 L4 questions. Reviewers checked the evidence available at the decision point, the applicable guideline, and whether the options supported determinate answer. L2 includes one explicit multiple-select item and L4 includes two; the other items are single choice. Multiple-select answers must match the complete reference set. The question specifies this requirement, and selecting only part of the set receives no credit. Reviewed rationales accompany all 350 L2/L4 items. Construction examples. Figure 3 shows shortened examples of the released task formats. The examples retain the answer labels and decision-relevant information; full inputs and reviewed rationales accompany the dataset. Data and code availability. De-identified benchmark inputs, multimodal assets, reference annotations, and supplementary control datasets are publicly available on Hugging Face; evaluation code and inference scripts are available on GitHub. sections.title: B Detailed Related Work
sections.content: Static medical QA and broad medical suites. Examination-style benchmarks such as MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, the medical subsets of MMLU, CMB, and CMExam have provided practical basis for assessing medical knowledge and localized reasoning skills [1720, 22, 23]. MultiMedQA and MedBench extended this approach by combining multiple medical QA datasets and testing more general medical reasoning across them [2, 21]. More recent benchmarksincluding MedHELM, MedXpertQA, and AnesSuites AnesBenchemphasize construct validity, specialtyspecific reasoning, and clinical abilities alongside exam-style performance [8, 24, 25]. NPCBench focuses on NPC and reports component performance and joint patient correctness separately. Multimodal medical evidence grounding. Medical MLLM evaluation has progressed beyond image-question datasets like VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and PathVQA toward benchmarks with broader modality coverage and greater clinical specialization [2628]. Frameworks such as OmniMedVQA, GMAI-MMBench, BenchX, CARES, and BrainMD assess dimensions including the breadth of 19 medical imaging modalities, model reliability, and cross-modality generalization [29, 33, 4850]. More domain-specific benchmarksEndoBench, DrVD-Bench, MedSG-Bench, MMOral, M3CoTBench, and MedThinkVQAtarget fine-grained image understanding, temporal or sequence-level grounding, and reasoning across multiple images [3032, 5153]. NPCBench examines these components in NPC, where pathology underpins diagnosis, MRI anatomy delineates local spread, sequence recognition shapes image interpretation, and assessment of local invasion guides staging and treatment intensity. Rubric-based and real-world clinical response evaluation. Open-ended clinical evaluation is increasingly grounded in explicit scoring rubrics and physician-validated criteria. HealthBench assesses multi-turn health-related dialogues using item-specific rubrics; LiveMedBench focuses on temporally separated clinical cases; LLMEval-Med incorporates physician adjudication combined with checklist-guided evaluation; MedDialogRubrics and ClinConsensus extend rubric-based assessment frameworks to consultation and longitudinal care scenarios [3438]. O1 ConsultRubrics uses the same criterion-level approach for NPC consultation, in which positive requirements capture key clinical conclusions, supporting patient evidence, and conditions that change the recommendation, whereas negative criteria differentiate between major and minor safety-critical errors. Workflow, longitudinal, and agentic clinical benchmarks. Workflow evaluations test information gathering, interaction, and decisions across multiple steps. MedJourney structures evaluation around the patient journey, whereas MedAgents, MDAgents, MedAgentsBench, and MedAgentBoard focus on collaborative problem-solving, tool integration, and multi-step clinical task execution [39, 41, 54 56]. In oncology, MTBBench emulates multidisciplinary tumor-board decision-making, and recent work on autonomous oncology agents investigates specialized workflows for treatment decision support [42, 57]. AgentClinic evaluates tool use and information gathering in simulated clinical encounters, while MedAgentBench tests tasks in FHIR-compatible electronic health record [40, 58]. Clinical-environment simulators additionally expose models to explicit state transitions [59]. NPCBench evaluates related questions within NPC: L5 tests decisions under different representations of longitudinal records, and L6 checks image labels and selected care answers for the same patient. Its primary care evaluation supplies clinical context without feeding previous care answers back, whereas separate serial controls test conversation retention. This distinction separates joint patient correctness from autonomous interaction with clinical environment.

sections.title: D Clinical Review and Judge Calibration
sections.content: NPC specialists reviewed each items clinical question, available evidence, reference answer, and scoring criteria. They checked staging, prior treatment, toxicity, organ function, and guideline assumptions, and standardized drug names, doses, units, and answer options. Future orders and outcomes were removed from inputs when they disclosed the target decision. Question-review outcomes and the six unscored CarePath cohort treatment questions appear in sections and C.3.5. D.1 Clinical Annotation and Adjudication In routine care, pathology and radiology examinations were initially interpreted by physician with 13 years of experience and finalized by senior subspecialist with more than five years of experience. Pathology reference labels were taken from finalized reports. For benchmark MRI annotation, another physician independently reviewed the examinations, reports, and staging criteria to assign structure-invasion and T-category labels. Three senior NPC radiation oncologists resolved disagreements by consensus. The independent benchmark review followed routine clinical reporting and preceded consensus adjudication. Review of clinical decisions. For L2, reviewers checked whether the vignette supplied the facts needed for one guideline decision and whether the answer options supported determinate choice. Missing variables, leading wording, and inconsistent guideline editions prompted revision. For L4, they assessed whether diagnosis, stage, treatment history, response, and contraindications supported the proposed management plan. The evaluated questions distinguish single-choice and explicit multiple-select items (section A). For L5, review preserved the order of clinical events after date normalization and restricted each question to evidence available at that checkpoint. Distractors differed in evidence use, treatment timing, toxicity management, or follow-up requirements. For O1, specialists separated essential conclusions, supporting case evidence, and conditional recommendations, then assigned major and minor error penalties according to clinical severity. D.2 Physician Calibration Audits Targeted Audit. For the automated O1 rubric judge, we constructed the Targeted Audit at the same criterion level as the scorer. The packet contained 811 criterion-level labels from 48 modelgenerated responses and was stratified to cover high judge disagreement, large score gaps, clinically safety-sensitive tags, and control cases with expected high or low rubric satisfaction. The physician worksheet marked responses whose completeness required review. Seventeen marked Gemini responses, comprising 263 criterion labels, were excluded because severe truncation prevented adjudication. Marked GPT-5.1 and GPT-OSS-120B responses remained eligible after physician confirmation that their individual criteria could still be judged. This left 548 criterion-level labels for the Targeted Audit agreement analysis. The retained set covers GPT-5.1, Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct, GPT-OSS-120B, and Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview responses, allowing calibration across both API and local response generators. The 548 labels include 286 from marked responses: 184 GPT-5.1 and 102 GPT-OSS-120B labels. Excluding these responses leaves 262 labels for sensitivity analysis, which gives the same judge ranking. The Expanded Audit broadens response-generator coverage, as described below. Qwen3.6-27B criterion judging uses non-thinking mode, temperature 0, top-p 1, and 768-token output limit. Outputs missing required fields are retried up to four times; three remaining Targeted Audit judgments use JSON-schema-constrained decoding with the same prompts and model. Expanded Audit. Physicians annotated 1,017 criteria from 54 responses generated by nine models on six cases: 859 labels were collected with generator identity hidden and 158 came from the Targeted Audit. Comparisons use the 1,013 criteria judged by all four models; four criteria without Qwen3.6-27B judgment are excluded from every judges comparison. Agreement is 77.6% for GPT-4.1, 70.5% for GPT-OSS-120B, 76.9% for Qwen3-30B, and 77.8% for Qwen3.6-27B, with Cohens κ of 0.547, 0.387, 0.538, and 0.544. The Targeted Audit (548 labels) and Expanded Audit (1,013 labels) are analysed separately because their response compositions differ. The primary O1 judge uses criterion-specific template with four calibration examples and explicit interpretation of requirements and errors. Define TP, FP, TN, and FN as the counts of (hℓ, ˆhℓ) = (1, 1), (0, 1), (0, 0), (1, 0), respectively; they sum to n. physician-positive label means the criterion is true. For negative error criterion, this means an error is present, not that the response is clinically correct. sections.content: These templates show the task instructions and response formats. Chinese-language instructions are rendered in English. Bracketed fields and ellipses stand for the full case text, options, or anatomical lists supplied in each request; images accompany the multimodal tasks. The O1 judge instructions and four calibration examples are reproduced below. The L2 and L4 cards show the single-choice format. One L2 item and two L4 items explicitly request multiple selections in the question; these require the complete reference option set, with no credit for missing or extra selections. Answer with the option letter from the given choices directly. Context [patient history up to this turn] Question At this decision point, which next action best matches guideline-concordant NPC specialist management? Options A. [action A] B. [action B] . . . Output the final answer directly. It must contain exactly one option letter inside boxed{}, for example boxed{A}. E.2 Multimodal Evidence Grounding Prompt A5. L3: Pathology overview Given the provided whole-slide pathology overview image, determine whether the case is nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Output only 0 or 1. 0 indicates normal tissue, and 1 indicates nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Prompt A6. L3: MRI sequence and plane You will see one NPC MRI sequence-recognition image composed of 33 panel. All nine images are slices from the same sequence of the same patient. Sequence names and explicit textual cues have been removed. Choose the matching joint sequence-plane class. Options A. T1_Ax; B. T2_Ax; C. T1+C_Ax; D. T1_COR; E. T1_SAG; F. T1+C_SAG; G. T1+C_COR_FS. Output only one option letter inside boxed{}, for example boxed{A}. Prompt A7. L3: MRI structure card You will see one NPC MRI structure card. The card is fixed 43 image. Each row corresponds to one MRI sequence, and each column contains one of three consecutive slices selected from the same sequence by maximizing the annotated structure-box area. The yellow rectangle marks the anatomical structure under evaluation. Row sequences [four sequence names in row order] Tasks Identify the base anatomical structure marked by the yellow box and output structure_id. Determine whether the structure is invaded and output invasion. Select the structure from [18 base-structure choices]. Left and right structures are collapsed for primary scoring. invasion is 0 (not invaded) or 1 (invaded). Response Output only one JSON object, without explanations, markdown, or code fences: {"structure_id":"nasal_passage", "invasion":0} Prompt A8. Each card has fixed 43 layout; the yellow rectangle marks the structure under evaluation. Tasks Determine invasion status for all 18 base anatomical structures. Integrate this evidence using the eighth edition AJCC/UICC TNM criteria for NPC and output the patient-level stage. structure_invasion must cover all 18 structures with value of 0 or 1. t_stage must be T1, T2, T3, or T4. Response Output only one JSON object, without explanations, markdown, or code fences: {"structure_invasion":{"nasal_passage":0, "oropharynx":0, "...":0}, "t_stage":"T1"} 45 Prompt A9. Coronal groups contain enhanced fat-suppressed T1 and precontrast non-fat-suppressed T1 at matched planes. Tasks Determine invasion status for all 18 base anatomical structures. Integrate this evidence using the eighth edition AJCC/UICC TNM criteria for NPC and output the patient-level stage. The structure list and JSON response fields are the same as in the structure-card T-stage task above. All selected image groups enter one request. Prompt A10. L3: staging from aligned sequence groups (400 patients) You will see axial and coronal MRI image groups from one NPC patient, with the same sequence arrangement described above. The axial coverage extends from the skull base to the inferior sternoclavicular joint. Task Determine the stage using the eighth edition AJCC/UICC TNM criteria for NPC. Response Output only one JSON object containing n_stage and the supporting imaging evidence. n_stage must be N0, N1, N2, or N3. E.3 CarePath episodes The pathology and MRI prompts produce diagnostic and staging predictions. Each care question receives the specified image-derived findings and clinical context. Earlier care answers are included only in the separate history-feedback experiments. The care prompt supplies the available clinical context, including N/M/overall-stage information in 133 questions. The clinical context and imageprediction fields jointly define the evidence available for the decision. Prompt A11. Infer the AJCC ninth-edition stage and briefly state the imaging evidence. The nasopharynx is recorded as the background primary site and excluded from structure-invasion scoring. Evaluate [18 candidate structures]. Response Output only JSON with the following fields: {"structure_invasion":{[structure]:0, ...}, "involved_structures":[...], "T_stage":"T1", "evidence":"[brief imaging evidence]"} T_stage must be T1, T2, T3, or T4. 46 Prompt A13. L6: Care decision Information is provided in clinical order. Answer using only the information available at the current decision point; do not assume findings absent from the question. Prior diagnostic findings [predicted pathology; predicted MRI stage and invaded structures; supplied N/M and overall-stage fields, where specified] Clinical information [available history and current checkpoint] Question [care decision] Options A. [action A]; B. [action B]; . . . ; [last option and action] Output only one option letter from [valid option letters]. E.4 Consultation Generation and Judging The response model sees the case and question. The judge additionally sees the generated answer and one signed criterion. true judgment earns credit for positive requirement and incurs deduction for negative error criterion. Prompt A14. O1: Consultation response You are assisting with nasopharyngeal carcinoma specialist consultation. Read the de-identified case information and answer the clinical question. Your answer should be clinically concise, evidence-grounded, and should state important uncertainty or missing information when relevant. Case [case_input] Question [question] Prompt A15. O1: Criterion judge You are evaluating an answer in nasopharyngeal carcinoma clinical consultation benchmark. Your job is to look at the case, the clinical question, the assistant response, and one rubric item. Judge whether the assistant response matches the rubric item according to the criterion type shown inside the rubric item. Case: [case] Question: [question] Assistant Response: [assistant_response] Rubric Item: [rubric_item] Instructions Return JSON object with exactly the following fields: "explanation" and "criteria_met". "criteria_met" must be boolean. "explanation" must be brief string explaining why the assistant response does or does not satisfy the rubric item. Refer to specific content from the assistant response when possible. Judge only the assistant response. Do not give credit for information that appears only in the case or question unless the assistant response also uses or states it. First identify the criterion type in the rubric item. For POSITIVE REQUIREMENT, return true only when all required elements are substantially satisfied by the assistant response. For NEGATIVE ERROR CRITERION, return true only if the assistant response actually makes the described mistake, unsafe recommendation, contradiction, or omission. Return false if the assistant avoids the error, gives the correct answer, or merely discusses the issue as caveat without committing the error. Prompt A15. O1: Criterion judge (continued) For NEGATIVE ERROR CRITERION, true judgment must be supported by specific offending content in the assistant response. If you cannot identify such content, return false. If negative criterion is about omission, such as "fails to mention" or "未说明", return true only when the required information is absent from the assistant response. If the rubric item uses phrases such as "such as", "for example", "including", "包括", "例如", or "如", the assistant response does not need to mention every example, but it must satisfy the core clinical concept. Accept clinically equivalent wording, synonyms, abbreviations, and reasonable Chinese-English variants. Do not require exact wording from the rubric item. Do not give extra credit for content outside the rubric item. For POSITIVE REQUIREMENT, if the response is vague, generic, or only partially satisfies the item, return false. If the assistant response contradicts the rubric item, return false. If the answer states uncertainty appropriately and the rubric item allows uncertainty or missing information, count that as satisfying the item. Calibration example 1 Calibration example 2 If the rubric item is "states that the adverse event is pruritus" and the assistant response says "the patient currently has skin itching", return: { "explanation": "The response identifies the current adverse event as skin itching, which is clinically equivalent to pruritus.", "criteria_met": true } If the rubric item is "states that the severity cannot be determined from the available information" and the assistant response directly assigns CTCAE grade 2 without explaining missing grading information, return: { "explanation": "The response gives specific CTCAE grade but does not state that severity cannot be determined from the available information.", "criteria_met": false } Calibration example 3 Calibration example Negative error criterion present. If the criterion type is NEGATIVE ERROR CRITERION, the rubric item is "incorrectly treats anemia as the main current adverse event", and the assistant response says "the main current adverse event is anemia", return: { "explanation": "The response identifies anemia as the main current adverse event, which matches the mistake described in the rubric item.", "criteria_met": true } Negative error criterion absent. If the criterion type is NEGATIVE ERROR CRITERION, the rubric item is "misclassifies cT3N0M0 as T4 or N-positive disease", and the assistant response correctly says "the clinical stage is cT3N0M0 because MRI supports T3 and there is no nodal or distant metastasis", return: { "explanation": "The response correctly states cT3N0M0 and does not misclassify the case as T4 or N-positive disease.", "criteria_met": false } Final instruction. Return only the JSON object. Do not include markdown fences or any other text.

sections.content: Identify the structure marked in yellow and determine whether it is invaded. Reference: nasal_passage; invasion=1. Identify the joint sequenceplane category from nine-slice panel with sequence-name cues removed. Reference: E, T1_SAG (sagittal T1). Patient-level staging. staging uses structure cards for 100 patients and aligned sequence groups for 300 patients. Both formats request all 18 base-structure invasion labels and T1T4 category under the eighth-edition AJCC/UICC criteria. staging uses sequence groups for disjoint cohort of 400 patients, with inferior coverage extending to the sternoclavicular joint. All images selected for patient enter one request; single card does not determine the final stage. F.1 Reading Model Responses The following responses illustrate why the scoring targets distinguish anatomical identity from invasion and distinguish an error criterion from positive requirement. Example 1: Anatomical identity and invasion Evaluation. GPT-5.1, MRI structure-identification experiment. Structure card. Atlas (C1 vertebra). Gold structure and invasion. atlas (C1 vertebra); invasion=0 Prediction. longus_capitis; invasion=0. Interpretation. The numeric invasion value matches, but refers to the wrong anatomical structure. The response fails the joint structureinvasion target; checking the binary value alone would miss this localization error. Example 2: An error criterion that is not triggered Context. In the physician-review packet, 60-year-old man with recurrent NPC after definitive chemoradiotherapy had received GP plus camrelizumab and was assessed as T3N1. The question asked for the current treatment strategy and guideline basis. Response. Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview proposed camrelizumab monotherapy maintenance (preferred systemic strategy), with additional workup and review of hepatitis and prior radiation dose. Error criterion. Choosing local radical treatment, such as re-irradiation or surgery, as the main strategy at this stage instead of systemic treatment. Interpretation. The response centres systemic treatment, so this criterion is false and incurs no deduction. This judgment concerns one criterion; the remaining requirements and errors must still be assessed before scoring the consultation.
